core_principles: Maintain a straight line from head to feet by stiffening the knee joints, hip joints, pelvis, and spine.
Allow the shoulders and elbows to flex and extend to raise and lower the body.
Ensure the scapulae retract and protract to facilitate glenohumeral range of motion.
Understand that knee push-ups shorten the lever, reducing bodyweight loading and core/prime mover requirements.
Vary hand positions to alter muscle recruitment: narrow base (50% shoulder width) increases triceps brachii and sternal head of pectoralis major activation.
common_mistakes: Failing to keep the body in a straight line (lack of stiffening of knees, hips, pelvis, and spine).
Flaring the elbows, particularly when performing narrow base push-ups, which orients movement into the transverse plane.
specific_findings: Knee push-up reduces bodyweight loading to 54% in the top position and 62% in the bottom position.
Standard push-up relative load is 69% of bodyweight in the top position and 75% of bodyweight in the bottom position.
Compressive spinal loading on L4/L5 during a standard push-up is 1,838 N.
Standard push-up prime mover mean muscle activation (normalized to MVC): Pectoralis major 61%, Triceps brachii 66%, Anterior deltoid 42%.

Standard push-up core muscle activation (normalized to MVC): Psoas 24%, External oblique 29%, Internal oblique 10%, Transverse abdominis 9%, Rectus abdominis 29%, Rectus femoris 10%, Erector spinae 3%.

Standard push-up upper-body stabilizer activation (normalized to MVC): Latissimus dorsi 11%, Biceps brachii 4%, Posterior deltoid 17%, Upper trapezius 45%, Middle trapezius 18%, Lower trapezius 27%, Serratus anterior 56%.
Hand width classifications: wide base (150% shoulder width), normal base (shoulder width), and narrow base (50% shoulder width).

core_principles: Shifting the torso forward relative to the hands increases pectoralis major activity and decreases triceps brachii activity.
Shifting the torso rearward relative to the hands slightly increases both pectoralis major and triceps brachii activity.
Elevating the feet increases the ground reaction force and overall load of the push-up.
Placing hands on an unstable surface (e.g., stability ball) increases triceps brachii and core activation compared to a stable surface at the same angle.
To maximize the muscle activation benefits of unstable surfaces, the hands should be placed on the unstable surface rather than the feet.
Elevating the feet above the hands provides a greater stimulus to the scapulothoracic stabilizing musculature than placing hands on a stability ball.
specific_findings: Push-up loads as a percentage of total body mass: hands elevated on a 61.0-cm box (41%), knee push-up (49%), hands elevated on a 30.5-cm box (55%), regular push-up (64%), feet elevated on a 30.5-cm box (70%), and feet elevated on a 61.0-cm box (74%).
BOSU push-ups increase the activity of the upper, mid, and lower trapezius fibers, but diminish serratus anterior activity.
EMG analysis failed to show any significant differences in muscle activation between the Perfect Push-up handgrips and standard push-ups.

core_principles: Countermovement push-ups (fast eccentric, reversal, and concentric phases without leaving the ground) are a safe and effective choice for explosive training because they maximize upper-body power without impact forces.
Clapping push-ups are highly effective for maximizing pectoralis major and triceps brachii muscle activation.
Advanced plyometric push-up variations should be avoided or used with extreme caution by individuals with pre-existing back issues due to high spinal loading.
Regress the push-up using wall push-ups or knee push-ups for individuals with limited upper-body strength.
Progress the push-up using single-arm/single-leg variations, weighted vests, elastic bands, chains, or unstable implements to increase difficulty.
common_mistakes: Performing advanced plyometric push-ups, such as alternating plyometric push-ups on a medicine ball, when having pre-existing back or lumbar spine issues.
specific_findings: An alternating plyometric push-up using a medicine ball has been shown to induce 6,224 N of compressive forces on the lumbar spine (6).

Clapping push-ups have been shown to outperform standard, slow eccentric, 1 hand on medicine ball, staggered hands, hands on 2 balls, 2 hands on 1 ball, rapid countermovement, 1 arm, and alternating plyometric push-up variations in pectoralis major and triceps brachii activity (6).
